video_title: Apollo’s Yahoo Playbook, 5 Years After the $5B Deal
gist: Yahoo CEO Jim Lanzone details how Apollo's ~$4.8B 2021 carve-out of Yahoo/AOL from Verizon was turned around via a GM-led conglomerate reorg, divestitures (Edgecast, ad-tech SSP, TechCrunch, AOL) and refocus on core consumer brands, already returning roughly Apollo's purchase price. He pitches Yahoo as an undervalued 700M-user, 75%-direct-traffic asset with its own data-grounded AI search engine (Yahoo Scout) and an eventual IPO or sale as the expected outcome.

insights.claim: Apollo bought Yahoo and AOL (Verizon Media) from Verizon for about $4.8B in a deal agreed May 2021 and closed September 2021; Verizon retained a 10% stake, and the combined assets had originally cost Verizon roughly twice that price.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Carve-out bought at ~50% of the strategic buyer's cost basis, with the seller retaining equity to bridge price.
insights.quote: They still own 10% of us

insights.claim: Apollo's Reed Raymond structured the Yahoo deal to return cash very quickly, and Yahoo has already paid back roughly Apollo's purchase price, making it one of the fastest-returning deals in Apollo's history.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Apollo is now 'playing with house money' on Yahoo; any IPO or sale is pure upside, a strong data point for PE tech carve-out playbooks.
insights.quote: It's the one of the fastest returning deals in the history of Apollo.

insights.claim: Lanzone argues Apollo did not run a cost-stripping PE playbook on Yahoo because it saw asymmetric upside, hiring a growth-oriented CEO; PE still wants an exit via IPO or sale rather than holding indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Selective PE owners treat high-traffic consumer assets as growth bets, not just cash-extraction vehicles.
insights.quote: there aren't that many that they view that have asymmetric upside relative to others where you just run the PE playbook

insights.claim: Under Verizon, Yahoo and AOL's mission was subordinated to helping Verizon grow 5G, so decisions were not driven by Yahoo's own consumer mission; the telco-owns-media vision (also AT&T/Time Warner) was right in concept but housed in the wrong company.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Telco-media conglomerates destroyed value; carve-outs from misaligned parents can unlock latent assets.
insights.quote: which is a really good vision but it was inside of the wrong company

insights.claim: Lanzone frames Yahoo as equivalent to any later-stage pre-IPO Silicon Valley company and says an outcome (IPO or sale) is expected by investors, though he has no IPO date to share.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Yahoo IPO or strategic sale is a likely future event to watch.
insights.quote: we're the same as any later stage preIPO Silicon Valley company

insights.claim: Lanzone expects Yahoo's revenue and profitability to be strong but roughly in an expected range at an eventual listing, with the main surprise being its healthy growth rate for a 30-year-old brand.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Signals a profitable, growing IPO candidate; growth rate is the key metric to scrutinize.
insights.quote: just maybe how healthy we are in growing, the rate at which we are growing

insights.claim: Lanzone's turnaround playbook spends the first six months evaluating the team and data rather than acting immediately, because the inside reality of products and audience always differs from the outside view.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Operator-led turnarounds front-load diagnosis; restructuring follows ~6-12 months after a change of control.
insights.quote: I don't come in guns blazing on on day one

insights.claim: Yahoo is a conglomerate of independently competing brands (Finance vs. Bloomberg/CNBC/WSJ/TradingView, Sports vs. ESPN, Mail vs. Gmail), unlike single-product peers Pinterest, Snap, Reddit and Roku.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Sum-of-the-parts valuation lens is appropriate; comps differ by unit.

insights.claim: Yahoo's first restructuring step in 2022 was reorganizing from Verizon-era functional silos (one head of product/tech/content across all brands) into GM-led divisions each with their own product, technology, content, and assigned sales/marketing.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Divisional GM structure enables faster execution and easier spin-offs or divestitures of units.

insights.claim: Lanzone admits he got conglomerate structure wrong at CBS Interactive by having all brands report to him as a product person, which slowed things down; he learned to hire entrepreneurial GMs and hold them accountable.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Founder-type CEOs centralizing product decisions is a scaling bottleneck in multi-brand companies.
insights.quote: I tried to have everything report to me

insights.claim: Every Yahoo general manager from Lanzone down has founded at least one company, a deliberate hiring choice for the turnaround's product team.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Entrepreneurial leadership bench signals growth orientation vs. maintenance mode.
insights.quote: Every general manager from me on down has been entrepreneur at least once

insights.claim: Lanzone's 'can't skip levels of the video game' framework: fix products first, then build new products from restored growth, then invest in brand marketing; marketing without great products is pointless.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Useful sequencing heuristic for evaluating turnaround progress.
insights.quote: you can't skip levels of the video game

insights.claim: Lanzone says the biggest mistake companies make at scale is falling asleep at the wheel with conservative, ladder-climbing non-product leaders; the decisive errors are invisible missed acquisitions, untaken chances and bad deals, which surface later as losses to startups.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Favor product-led management teams at incumbents; non-product leadership is a leading indicator of disruption risk.
insights.quote: the chances they didn't take, the company they didn't buy, maybe the thing that they sold

insights.claim: Lanzone's prior turnarounds: Ask Jeeves (stock up 50x before sale to IAC), CBS Interactive (grew users from 70M to 220M; CBS stock went from about $3 to nearly $80), and a brief Tinder stint during COVID.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Track record of the operator underwrites the Yahoo thesis.
insights.quote: We we 50xed that stock and sold it to IEC and Barry Diller.

insights.claim: Yahoo divested Edgecast (a CDN competing with Akamai) as a business it had no right to operate, and later TechCrunch and AOL (sold October of last year), focusing on core consumer brands.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Portfolio pruning was central to rapid cash return to Apollo.

insights.claim: AOL and Yahoo had each bought 30+ ad-tech companies, leaving an SSP/DSP/native stack that lost hundreds of millions of dollars a year and forced Yahoo to take ads only from its own ad tech, preventing yield optimization on Yahoo's pages.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Captive in-house ad tech can depress publisher yield; unbundling unlocked both cost savings and revenue.
insights.quote: it was hundreds of millions of dollars a year out the door that we had to fix

insights.claim: In February 2023 Yahoo laid off over 2,000 people, partly by shutting down its SSP rather than selling it so no buyer would get preferential access to Yahoo inventory; it sold the native business to Taboola for a 25% stake.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Yahoo holds a ~25% stake in Taboola, a material equity link; open yield optimization was prioritized over sale proceeds.
insights.quote: in February 2023, we actually had to let go of over 2,000 people

insights.claim: Yahoo kept and invested in its DSP as a 'crown jewel,' and says the DSP won nine out of ten head-to-head tests against rivals thanks to Yahoo's first-party audience data.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: First-party-data-driven DSP is a differentiated ad-tech asset in a post-cookie market.
insights.quote: we went nine out of 10 head-to-head tests

insights.claim: Yahoo shifted news from enterprise journalism (White House correspondents, breaking news competing with the AP) back to aggregation, where it is a top-three property, and to decision-supporting analysis content such as fantasy and stock-market analysts.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Lower-cost aggregation plus utility content improves margins versus original reporting.

insights.claim: Yahoo reaches about 700 million monthly users, with Yahoo Sports and Yahoo Finance each over 100 million monthly users and Yahoo Mail used by one-third of Americans; it ranks top five in the US monthly.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Massive owned audience underpins advertising and new-product distribution.
insights.quote: all those things to fit together are what add up to 700 million users a month

insights.claim: About 75% of Yahoo's users come directly rather than via SEO, and about 75% are logged in on a given day, which Lanzone says makes Yahoo unusually effective for advertisers.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Low dependence on Google SEO reduces AI-search traffic risk; logged-in data supports premium ad pricing.
insights.quote: 75% of our users are coming directly to Yahoo

insights.claim: Over 50% of Yahoo's audience is Gen Z and Millennial, 75% of Gen Z uses a Yahoo product, and marketing campaigns produced a 31-point absolute lift in Gen Z brand love; Mail's fastest growth is from Gen Z.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Contradicts the 'legacy aging audience' narrative; supports long-duration value.
insights.quote: 75% of Gen Z is using Yahoo

insights.claim: Lanzone argues that new brands enter the top internet rankings only every 3-5 years (ChatGPT most recently, before that TikTok, Snap, Instagram), so inherited distribution lets incumbents improve products and have it work, while startups must 'light the wet log.'
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Distribution scarcity favors incumbents with traffic; AI does not easily displace top-traffic consumer properties.
insights.quote: new brands that get added to that really only happen once every 3 to 5 years

insights.claim: Lanzone says some startups are valued higher than Yahoo despite having less than 0.1% of its user base, and AI search startups were valued at 6x Yahoo despite Yahoo's larger search volume, revenue and profit; he considers Yahoo one of the most undervalued assets.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Signals stretched private-market valuations and a potential valuation arbitrage for Yahoo at IPO.
insights.quote: there are companies that are valued more than us who have less than one tenth of 1% of our user base

insights.claim: High startup valuations prevent Yahoo from making large mergers, so it buys small startups for their products and talent, whose people now lead key initiatives.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Expect tuck-ins rather than large Yahoo M&A while private valuations stay high.

insights.claim: Yahoo's new college fantasy football product drew users of whom 40% were brand new to Yahoo, and Yahoo Fantasy had its three biggest days ever this year for NFL.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: New products are acquiring incremental users, evidence of growth beyond the legacy base.
insights.quote: college 40% of those users are brand new to Yahoo

insights.claim: Yahoo Scout, launched earlier this year, is Yahoo's first own search engine in 17 years; it grounds Yahoo's own data (30 years of search history, publisher data, knowledge graph, user data) and sends it to a lightweight LLM (Anthropic's Haiku at launch, others now) for answers.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Model-agnostic, data-grounded AI search lets a non-frontier player compete cheaply; a demand signal for small inference models.
insights.quote: At launch it was Haiku.

insights.claim: Lanzone says outsourcing search largely to Microsoft for 17 years left Yahoo vulnerable in one of its most important revenue streams, so owning search again was strategically 'life-changing.'
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Reduced dependence on Microsoft/Bing for search economics; watch revenue-share implications.
insights.quote: that left us in a really vulnerable position

insights.claim: Lanzone calls Yahoo's 'original sin' outsourcing search (to Inktomi, then Google) in June 2000 as a cost center, when 92% of internet sessions started with search and before paid-search business models existed.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Outsourcing a strategic core because it lacks a current business model is a recurring incumbent error, relevant to AI today.
insights.quote: The original sin of Yahoo was giving search away to Google in June of 2000.

insights.claim: Yahoo remains the third-ranked US search engine and is a top-20 publisher whose content was taken by LLMs without permission, but its real-time categories were less exposed than evergreen content.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Real-time content is more defensible against LLM disintermediation than evergreen content.
insights.quote: we're still the third ranked search engine in the US

insights.claim: Lanzone attributes Yahoo's positive brand perception relative to AI companies seen as 'evil' to not building a frontier LLM, and says Yahoo partners with rather than competes against publishers by sending them traffic.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Brand trust can be a differentiator as AI incumbents face backlash.
insights.quote: it's because we're not building a large language model

insights.claim: Because AI agent products all first ask for email and calendar access, Lanzone sees Yahoo Mail, as a trusted personal 'vault of your life,' as a strategic position in the agent era, focused on consumers while Gmail and Outlook are enterprise-oriented.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Consumer email is a key data asset for agentic AI; Yahoo may launch consumer agent features.
insights.quote: every one of these new agent products, the first thing they ask is, can we have access to your email and calendar?

insights.claim: Yahoo's mission, being the trusted guide to the internet for personal goals, explicitly excludes enterprise/B2B and serves as a filter against chasing trends like AI coding, assistants or neocloud pivots; future added brands need not be Yahoo-branded but must fit it.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Signals no B2B/infrastructure diversification; acquisitions likely consumer-utility brands.
insights.quote: we're not going to be a an enterprise or B2B company

insights.claim: Lanzone declines to time the market top, noting that since the mid-2010s repeated crash calls were wrong and taking chips off the table would have been a mistake, while asserting Yahoo is resilient enough to weather a downturn.
insights.speaker: Jim Lanzone
insights.so_what: Operator view: avoid timing bubbles; resilience over prediction.
insights.quote: if you tried to take your chips off the table at any point in time
